nearest_prs.assessment: Accepted: hold a nut flat behind a plate with one hand while the other drives a screw into it until snug. Shares the hold-one-part, turn-the-other bimanual pattern. Ours differs in what is held and why: the held part is a loose rotating assembly whose angle must be set (lifted 15 degrees to level) and kept while the nut's thread drag would swing it; the turned part is a hex nut on a horizontal axis just inside a 12 cm-deep tank wall; the thread is left-hand; and the turn must stop at a snug seat with an overtightening fail.

Accepted rotary can opener: one hand keeps handles squeezed while the other turns the key in regrasped part-turns. Same hold-and-turn family, different object, mechanism and goal (continuous cut vs a bounded seat with angle setting).

Accepted compression joint with a spanner a set turn past snug. Shares the 'past snug but not too far' window; ours is a bare-gripper turn of a plastic locknut with a held counterpart, no spanner, no olive/pipe assembly.

Final reject: locknut with restricted wrench swing, rejected for occupational importance (not 500k core work). Warns that a generic locknut tightening needs a strong importance frame; ours is pitched as Societal relatability (common household toilet-handle fix) with Kohler and home-repair sources.

Final reject: raised toilet seat install judged specialist home-care, and a 50 N force not checkable. Ours is the common loose/drooping flush handle fix; real-trial scoring uses angle marks and video, no force reading.

Final reject: clearing a toilet rim jet judged hidden maintenance. Importance risk for ours: the locknut is inside the tank, though the symptom (a wobbly drooping handle) is visible and commonly fixed by householders.
Pending steering-lock: turn the wheel off the bolt and hold while the key turns. Hold-and-turn pattern, entirely different object and mechanism.

physical_skill: Bimanual counter-hold: one gripper lifts a loose trip-lever handle 15 degrees to level and holds it against the drag of the thread while the other gripper, reaching down inside the open tank behind its front wall, turns a hex locknut counterclockwise (left-hand thread) a quarter turn to snug, stopping before 30 degrees past snug, then both release clear.
valid_shortcuts: Any grip on the handle or escutcheon that holds the assembly level is valid; the scorer reads only angles and final fingertip clearance.
Any number of regrasps or turn increments on the nut is valid, as is turning the nut by pushing a flat rather than pinching.
Seating the nut with the handle crooked and then not being able to re-level scores 0.5 by design (the nut clamps the assembly).
One-arm turning was red-teamed: the nut's drag swings the loose handle instead of advancing the nut (0.0). Overtightening (34 degrees past snug) scores 0.0. Doing nothing scores 0.0.
Distractors are ignored; moving them is allowed.
distinct_from_nearest: No accepted or pending task in the refreshed inventory involves a toilet flush handle, trip lever or its tank locknut; the only live toilet task (#1847) is a toilet-roll spindle. The nearest skill match (#618, hold a nut behind a plate while driving a screw) differs in that our held part is a free-rotating assembly whose angle must be actively set and maintained against thread drag, the nut is turned on a horizontal axis just inside a tank wall, the thread is left-hand, and the seat window (within 3 degrees of snug, fail beyond 30 degrees past) carries the manufacturer's do-not-overtighten warning. #1851 and #1562 share the hold-and-turn and past-snug window motifs only in general form. This is a reasoned novelty assessment, not an acceptance guarantee.
importance_risk: Reviewers have closed toilet maintenance tasks as hidden or specialist (#2547 rim jet, #2782 raised seat) and generic locknut tightening for occupational scale (#2262). Our frame is Societal relatability: a loose, drooping flush handle is a common household fault with a standard DIY fix documented by Kohler and mainstream home-repair guides; the sources establish the operation, not a measured frequency.
